Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion

When I remember the event I feel intense rage

issues.explanation: The trigger 'Arab villages' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of physical abuse by a romantic partner and the rest of the profile, which centers on interpersonal abuse-related cues, self-appraisals, and memory phenomena. Without any corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal content involving war, military, or ethnic/geographic conflict, this item appears clinically incoherent for this patient.

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Strictly restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other selected items coherently describe PTSD related to partner physical abuse (criticism, violence, offender cues; fragmented/alien memory; rage; dehumanization, self-blame, emotional numbing; distraction and cue avoidance). In contrast, restrictive eating introduces a distinct control-focused coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in triggers, memory, threat, or appraisals, making it clinically hard to explain as part of the same formulation rather than a separate problem.

vignette:
Matiu Hale is a 74-year-old editor who came to treatment months after ending a violent relationship that had unfolded largely behind the closed door of his apartment and, at times, in the office where he still works part-time reviewing manuscripts. He is a divorced American man of Oceanian background, careful with language and usually measured in how he presents himself, but when he first began describing what had happened with his former partner, his account came in stark visual fragments rather than a flowing story. He spoke of a hand gripping his shirtfront, of the sudden change in the other man's face when a disagreement turned, of being shoved into the edge of a table, of the look in his partner's eyes when he corrected him or tried to defend himself. The scenes arrived as isolated pictures, as if each were sealed off from the next. Even as he described them, he said the memories felt strangely unreal, as though he were reciting something that had happened to somebody else. Yet certain images carried such force that he would clench his jaw and say he could feel a blast of rage rising in him the instant they came back.

The violence had often erupted around criticism, sometimes over trivial things. Matiu had spent his career refining sentences, noticing imprecision, making corrections gently but automatically. In the relationship, that ordinary habit became dangerous terrain. If he pointed out a mistake, questioned a story, or even sounded too exacting, he learned to watch his partner's expression for signs of a turn. What stays with him now are those condensed moments: his own voice stopping mid-sentence, the scrape of a chair, the first shove, the instant of realizing that being right or being careful with words offered no protection. Over time he had come to believe the assaults said something essential about him. He did not describe himself as unlucky; he was certain the abuse happened because of the sort of person he was. In session he spoke with shame about being "the kind of man things are done to," and there was a flatness when he said that during the relationship he had felt less like a person than like an object being handled, moved, and used.

After the relationship ended, his life narrowed around reminders he could not bear. Because seeing his former partner was one of the sharpest jolts, he changed grocery stores, stopped going to a café they had frequented, and planned his routes through town to reduce the chance of running into him. He was not only avoiding the man himself, but anything attached to him strongly enough to bring him to mind. At work, where editorial exchange depends on correction and critique, he found himself thrown by even ordinary interactions. If a younger colleague challenged one of his edits or an author pushed back on his comments, his body would tense before he had fully registered why. Being corrected, even politely, no longer felt like a routine professional exchange; it carried the immediate sting of threat. On those days he would turn away from the conversation as quickly as he could, open another document, busy himself with formatting, answer emails compulsively, or find some small technical task to bury himself in until the feeling passed.

He did the same with emotion more broadly. He had become wary of any strong feeling, not only fear but sadness, tenderness, even excitement, because intensity itself seemed unsafe. If grief or anger began to surface, he redirected himself into work, television, crossword puzzles, anything that would keep his mind moving sideways. He described this not as a choice he liked, but as the only way he knew to get through the day without being overtaken. Still, the cost had become plain. Friends noticed he was harder to reach and less animated. He stayed detached during conversations and cut visits short. In quieter moments he was haunted by the conviction that normal feeling was gone for good, that whatever range of emotion he once had had been blunted beyond repair.

What finally brought Matiu in was a recent incident in the office. A senior colleague, meaning no harm, marked up one of his edits in red and said, "I think this needs tightening." Matiu felt himself go rigid. For a second he did not see the page in front of him but one of those fixed images from the relationship, and with it came a surge of furious heat so strong he had to leave the room. He spent the rest of the day pretending to reorganize files so no one would ask what was wrong. That frightened him almost as much as the memory itself. He is seeking help now because he no longer wants his world arranged around evasion, nor does he want to keep living as if he were something less than fully human. At the same time, what frightens him most is the possibility that his shame is true-that this says something permanent about his character-and that he may never again feel like himself rather than a hollowed-out version watching his own life from a distance.
